slides.notes:
**Open with a question, not a fact.**
- "How many of you composted last night?" — pause, let the hands stay down.
- "In Seoul, you would have. Not because you're better people — because the bin weighs your trash and bills you for it."

**Set the frame:**
- This is not a travel brochure. One of Seoul's flagship policies is actively failing right now, in 2026 — and that failure is the most useful thing in this presentation.
- Promise the payoff: "By the end I want you to leave with five specific things New York should steal."

**Timing:** \~1 min. You should finish this slide by 0:01.

- Seoul \~9.4M city / \~26M metro · NYC \~8.3M city / \~20M metro
- Both hyper-dense, vertical, **apartment-dominant**, and out of developable land
- **Buildings = 67% of Seoul's GHG · 66–71% of NYC's** (the range is because NYC inventories differ by year)
- Each city has one flagship climate law: Seoul's Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality; NYC's Local Law 97

**The divergence — this is the whole talk:**
- **Seoul lends at 1.75%. NYC fines at $268 per ton.**
- "Hold that difference in your head for the next half hour. Everything else is a consequence of it."

**Transition:** "So why buildings? Look at the split."

- Seoul's 2005 baseline: **52.34 million tons CO₂e** — the figure the −50% target is measured from
- **Buildings 67%**; buildings + transport together **85%**

**Say the caveat out loud — it builds credibility:**
- Seoul's own 2020 release said 68.2%; a UNESCAP paper said 68.8% on 2018 data. **"Roughly two-thirds" is what's actually defensible.** I'll flag disagreeing sources throughout, because they disagree often.

**Why this matters to us specifically:**
- 67% from buildings means **the design professions own this problem** — not utilities, not transit agencies. Us.
- "And almost all of those buildings are already standing. We don't get to design our way out with new work."

**Timing:** \~1 min — this is a short slide. Move briskly.

**1977–78 — the first emergency:**
- 1977: embankment joins Nanjido island to the mainland. 1978: it becomes Seoul's official dump — chosen for access and distance from downtown
- Waste piled to **\~90 m** in two mounds. **Korea had no landfill gas or leachate treatment at the time** — it vented methane and toxic gas into the city
- 1993: city closes it and begins stabilization

**2011 — the second emergency:**
- Fukushima, plus a city-wide blackout in Seoul the same year
- **National energy self-sufficiency is 22.1% — 35th of 38 OECD countries.** Korea imports almost all its energy.

**The line to land:**
- "Seoul's sustainability policy was not born from idealism. It was born from a garbage mountain and a power failure."
- Worth remembering when we ask what actually motivates cities to act.

**Transition:** "Out of that came a plan with real dates in it."
